note: The A1 teaching order, hand-written. Read docs/CURRICULUM.md before changing it — the order is the design, not a list.

units.title: Ich heiße Miriam
canDo: introduce yourself and ask someone's name
say where you're from
greet and say goodbye at any time of day
units.grammarNote: sein, heißen and kommen are the three verbs a first conversation needs, before any rule about conjugation patterns exists to teach.

scenario.role: someone new at a language-exchange evening
scenario.goal: introduce yourself and find out their name

options.say: Ich heiße Sam. Und wie heißt du?

options.why: That answers a greeting, not the question "what's your name".

dialogue.them: Ich heiße Lena. Woher kommst du?

options.why: heißen is for names; woher kommst du asks where you're from.

units.title: Was machst du beruflich?
canDo: say what your job is
ask what someone does for work
say if you're married or have children
units.grammarNote: Regular verb conjugation across all persons, once ich/du/er has already been met through sein and heißen, so the pattern has something to generalise from.

scenario.goal: talk about what you both do and where you live

options.why: That answers where you live, not what you do for work.

dialogue.them: Ich arbeite als Verkäuferin. Wohnst du hier in der Stadt?

options.why: That's true information, maybe, but it doesn't answer whether you live in the city.

units.title: Das ist meine Schwester
canDo: introduce your family members
say what languages you speak
answer yes, no, or actually with ja / nein / doch
units.grammarNote: mein and dein, plus ja/nein/doch, arrive once there is a family to point at and a reason to correct a wrong guess about it.

scenario.role: a friend looking at a family photo with you
scenario.goal: explain who's who and what languages they speak
scenario.opener: Wer ist das? Ist das deine Schwester?

dialogue.them: Wer ist das? Ist das deine Schwester?

options.why: The question was about a Schwester (sister) — answering "yes, that's my brother" doesn't match.

options.say: Ja, sie spricht sehr gut Englisch.

options.why: The question was about a language, not about who she is.

units.title: Das Bild ist so schön
canDo: name the furniture in a room using der / die / das
ask how much something costs and say if it's expensive
replace a noun with er / es / sie
units.grammarNote: der/die/das and the pronouns that stand in for them, taught together because a pronoun with no article behind it is a guess.

scenario.role: a friend shopping with you for furniture
scenario.goal: say what you think of a piece and ask the price
scenario.opener: Schau mal, der Schrank! Wie findest du ihn?

dialogue.them: Schau mal, der Schrank! Wie findest du ihn?

options.say: Ich finde, er ist sehr schön.
Ich finde, sie ist sehr schön.
options.why: der Schrank is masculine, so it's replaced by er, not sie.
The question asks for a price, not an opinion.

units.title: Ist das ein Tisch?
canDo: describe an everyday object by its material and colour
say you don't have something with kein
ask what something is called in German
units.grammarNote: kein completes the negation nicht started in unit 2, once there is a concrete noun — a missing key, a missing chair — worth negating.

scenario.role: a flatmate who can't find their things
scenario.goal: help them work out what's missing

options.why: That names a different object entirely, not an answer about the key.

dialogue.them: Und meine Brille? Sie ist blau.

options.say: Ich sehe keine blaue Brille hier.

options.why: That's true of a bottle, but nobody asked about a bottle.

units.title: Wir haben einen Termin
canDo: name office equipment
say what you need using the accusative
talk about one item versus several with plurals
units.grammarNote: The accusative arrives early, Momente's own pace: ich brauche and ich suche need an object from the first office-vocabulary lesson.

scenario.role: a colleague setting up for a meeting
scenario.goal: say what's missing and what you need
scenario.opener: Wo ist der Kalender? Ich brauche ihn.

dialogue.them: Wo ist der Kalender? Ich brauche ihn.

options.say: Ich suche einen Stift, keinen Kalender.

options.why: Nobody asked about a password — the topic is the missing Kalender.
brauchen takes the accusative, so der becomes den.

units.title: Sie können super tanzen!
canDo: say what you can and can't do
talk about your hobbies and how often you do them
pay someone a compliment
units.grammarNote: können and the Satzklammer it forces, taught through hobbies because ability is the first thing worth saying with a second verb.

scenario.goal: find out what they can do and compliment them

options.say: Ich kann gut kochen und ich schwimme manchmal.

options.why: kann is for ich; kannst is for du.

dialogue.them: Ich tanze jeden Tag — schau mal!

options.say: Wow, du kannst wirklich super tanzen!

options.why: True or not, that's not the compliment the moment calls for.

units.title: Ich habe leider keine Zeit
canDo: suggest an activity and agree on a time
name the days of the week and parts of the day
say you don't have time
units.grammarNote: Verb-second is stated explicitly here, once a fronted time phrase like am Samstag gives the subject a reason to move.

scenario.goal: suggest something and settle on when
scenario.opener: Gehen wir am Samstag ins Kino?

dialogue.them: Gehen wir am Samstag ins Kino?

options.say: Ja, gern! Um wie viel Uhr?
Am Samstag ich habe keine Zeit.
options.why: The finite verb has to come second: Am Samstag habe ich keine Zeit.

options.say: Ich weiß nicht, wo das Kino ist.
options.why: That dodges the actual question, which was about the time.

units.title: Ich mag Hamburger
canDo: say what food you like and don't like
order food and drink in a café
use möchte to ask politely
units.grammarNote: möchte, mögen and essen together, because ordering food is the first genuinely polite request the course asks for.

scenario.goal: order something to eat and drink

options.say: Ich möchte einen Kaffee und ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.

options.why: You were asked what you'd like — saying what you dislike doesn't place an order.

dialogue.them: Und dazu vielleicht Käse oder Fleisch?

options.say: Nein danke, ich esse keinen Käse.

options.why: Tea wasn't offered here — the question was about cheese or meat.

units.title: Wann kommst du denn an?
canDo: talk about how you're travelling and when you'll arrive
use separable verbs like ankommen and abholen
ask someone to pick you up
units.grammarNote: Separable verbs, taught through arrival and pickup: ankommen and abholen are exactly the two a learner needs for a first real trip.

scenario.role: a friend you're visiting by train
scenario.goal: tell them your travel plan and when you land

options.say: Ich komme um sechs Uhr am Bahnhof an.

options.why: With a separable verb, the prefix goes to the end: Ich komme ... an.

options.say: Ja, ich steige in den Zug ein.
options.why: That describes what you're doing, not whether they should pick you up.

units.title: Was hast du gestern gemacht?
canDo: say what you did yesterday using the Perfekt with haben
talk about your daily routine in the past
ask when a shop or office is open
units.grammarNote: The Perfekt with haben, so a learner can finally answer was hast du gemacht about their own day, not just describe the present.

scenario.role: a friend checking in on your day
scenario.goal: say what you got up to yesterday

options.say: Ich habe eingekauft und dann einen Spaziergang gemacht.
Ich habe eingekauft und dann ich habe spazieren gemacht.
options.why: Two Perfekt clauses joined with und share one habe — no need to repeat it.

dialogue.them: Und heute? Hast du eine Pause gemacht?

options.say: Ja, ich habe eine Pause gemacht und Zeitung gelesen.
Ja, ich mache gestern eine Pause.
options.why: Something already finished needs the Perfekt (habe gemacht), not the present tense.

units.title: Im Frühling bin ich nach Hamburg gefahren
canDo: say where you went using the Perfekt with sein
talk about the seasons and months
describe a festival or trip you took
units.grammarNote: The Perfekt with sein closes A1.1 on purpose: it needs haben's shape already fixed, and a trip is the natural moment to introduce it.

scenario.goal: tell them about a trip you took
scenario.opener: Warst du letztes Jahr im Urlaub?

dialogue.them: Warst du letztes Jahr im Urlaub?

options.say: Ja, im Sommer bin ich nach Hamburg gefahren.
Ja, im Sommer ich habe nach Hamburg gefahren.
options.why: fahren takes sein in the Perfekt, and the finite verb still needs position two: bin ich gefahren.

dialogue.them: Und was habt ihr da gefeiert?

options.why: feiern is a regular verb taking an object, so its Perfekt uses haben, not sein.

units.title: Der Akkusativ
canDo: use den, die, das and die as objects
say what you see, have and need
notice that only masculine changes
units.grammarNote: The first case shift, and the whole of A1.2 leans on it. Only der becomes den — saying that plainly removes most of the fear.

scenario.role: a flatmate who has lost something
scenario.goal: say what you are looking for and found

options.why: The object takes the accusative: den Schlüssel.
Feminine stays die in the accusative.
einen needs a noun after it.

units.title: Einkaufen
canDo: ask for an amount of something
ask what something costs
pay and understand the change
units.grammarNote: Accusative where you actually meet it: ich nehme den Käse.

scenario.goal: buy two things and pay
scenario.opener: Guten Tag! Das macht acht Euro.

options.why: A gram of apples is nothing. Use Kilo.
Water comes in a Flasche, not a Packung.

options.say: Hier, bitte. Brauche ich eine Tüte?

options.why: Say what you mean: das ist billig.

units.title: Wo ist das?
canDo: ask the way
understand left, right and straight on
say where something is
units.grammarNote: Static place prepositions only. The two-way ones wait for unit 39, after the dative exists.

scenario.role: a stranger who has stopped you
scenario.goal: give directions

options.why: weit says how far, not which way.
zwischen needs two things to be between.

options.say: Nein, er ist neben dem Café.

options.why: bei takes a place, not a direction.

units.title: In der Stadt
canDo: name the places in a town
say where you are going
say what you do there
units.grammarNote: zum/zur as fixed forms. They are contractions of a dative that has not been taught, and pretending otherwise would be a lie a learner catches later.

scenario.goal: say what is where

options.say: Die Bank ist neben dem Rathaus.
Die Apotheke ist neben dem Rathaus.
options.why: A pharmacy sells medicine, not money.
You were asked where to eat.
Post is feminine: zur Post.

units.title: Können und müssen
canDo: say what you can do
say what you have to do
put the second verb at the end
units.grammarNote: The bracket — modal second, infinitive last — is the structural idea of German. Two modals first, not all six.

scenario.role: a colleague who needs a hand
scenario.goal: say what you can and must do

options.why: After können the verb stays in the infinitive: helfen.
After müssen it is the infinitive: arbeiten.

options.say: Vielleicht. Es ist nicht nötig möglich.
options.why: Say one: nötig or möglich.

units.title: Wollen, möchten, dürfen
canDo: say what you want
ask permission politely
tell the difference between wollen and möchten
units.grammarNote: möchten becomes a modal here, having been a fixed phrase since unit 15. Ich will can sound blunt to a German ear; that is worth saying out loud.

scenario.role: someone in a place with rules
scenario.goal: say what is allowed

options.why: verboten and erlaubt are opposites.
wollen is wanting; permission is dürfen.
One modal is enough.

units.title: Trennbare Verben
canDo: use a separable verb in a sentence
put the prefix at the end
recognise which prefixes separate
units.grammarNote: Straight after the modal bracket, because it is the same idea: the meaningful part goes last.

scenario.goal: arrange when things start

options.why: Separable verbs split: ich stehe … auf.
Again it splits: es fängt … an.

options.say: Ja, ich komme mit. Ich rufe dich an.

options.why: ich komme mit.

units.title: Die Wohnung
canDo: name the rooms and the furniture
describe where you live
say what is in a room
units.grammarNote: es gibt takes the accusative, which is unit 21 doing real work.

scenario.goal: ask about the rooms and the rent

options.say: Es gibt auch einen Balkon, oder?
Es gibt auch ein Balkon, oder?
options.why: es gibt takes the accusative: einen Balkon.

dialogue.them: Ja, und hier ist die Küche.

options.why: In a question the verb comes first: gibt es.

options.say: Und wie viel ist die Miete?
Und wie viel ist der Vermieter?
options.why: The Vermieter is the person. You mean the Miete.

units.title: Der Dativ
canDo: use dem, der and den as indirect objects
say who you give something to
use mir and dir
units.grammarNote: The second case, eight units after the first. Introduced through people rather than through a table.

scenario.goal: say who gets what

options.why: The person receiving takes the dative: dir.
gehören always takes the dative: mir.
schmecken takes the dative: mir.

units.title: Termine machen
canDo: make an appointment on the phone
suggest and refuse a time
cancel politely
units.grammarNote: The first Alltag-shaped unit. Uses time from unit 10, days from 11, modals from 25.

scenario.goal: make an appointment

options.why: The Praxis is the surgery. You want a Termin.
gestern is in the past.
absagen cancels it. You have just booked it.

units.title: Beim Arzt
canDo: name the parts of the body
say what hurts
understand what the doctor asks
units.grammarNote: mir tut der Kopf weh — dative where German insists on it and English does not.

scenario.role: a doctor asking what is wrong
scenario.goal: describe where it hurts

options.why: The verb is already there: tut weh.
Say one thing at a time.

options.say: Danke. Nehme ich die Tablette morgens?
Danke. Nehme ich das Bein morgens?
options.why: Bein is your leg, not the medicine.

units.title: Perfekt mit haben
canDo: say what you did
form the participle of a regular verb
put it at the end
units.grammarNote: The spoken past, and the third use of the bracket. ge- -t for regular verbs; the strong ones are learnt as they come.

scenario.goal: say what you did at the weekend
scenario.opener: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?

options.why: The Perfekt needs the participle: gearbeitet.
The participle is gelesen.

options.say: Ja, und ich habe viel gegessen!
Ja, und ich habe viel essen!
options.why: The participle is gegessen.

units.title: Perfekt mit sein
canDo: say where you went
choose between haben and sein
talk about your weekend
units.grammarNote: Movement and change of state take sein. A short closed list, so it is worth learning as a list.

scenario.role: a friend you have not seen
scenario.goal: say where you went

options.why: Movement takes sein: ich bin gefahren.
kommen is movement: ich bin gekommen.

options.say: Heute bin ich zu Hause geblieben.
Heute habe ich zu Hause geblieben.
options.why: bleiben takes sein: ich bin geblieben.

units.title: Das Wetter
canDo: say what the weather is doing
name the seasons and months
understand a forecast
units.grammarNote: A vocabulary breather between the two past tenses and the harder second half.

scenario.goal: talk about the weather

options.say: Es ist kalt und es regnet.
Es ist kalt und es Regen.
options.why: Regen is the noun; the verb is regnet.

options.say: Morgen ist es Sonne sonnig warm.
options.why: One word is enough: sonnig.
Snow and warm do not go together.

units.title: Kleidung
canDo: name what you are wearing
say what suits you
ask for another size
units.grammarNote: Still predicative. Attributive endings are deliberately not A1 and the course says so rather than half-teaching them.

scenario.goal: try something on and change the size

options.why: umtauschen is for something you already bought.
rot is a colour, not a size.

options.say: Sie ist zu klein. Haben Sie sie größer?
Sie ist zu klein. Ich trage sie.
options.why: If it is too small you do not want to wear it.

units.title: Unterwegs
canDo: buy a ticket
say how you travel
understand an announcement
units.grammarNote: mit dem Bus — the dative from unit 29 in the phrase you use every day.

scenario.goal: work out which train and when

options.why: A train leaves from a Gleis; a bus from a Haltestelle.

options.say: Ja, in Hannover steigst du um.
Ja, in Hannover steigst du ein.
options.why: einsteigen is getting on at the start; changing is umsteigen.
A delay is not something you need.

units.title: Der Imperativ
canDo: tell somebody to do something
ask for something politely
understand a written instruction
units.grammarNote: du, ihr and Sie forms. The Sie form is what you meet on signs and in offices, so it comes first here.

scenario.role: a friend who is about to do something risky
scenario.goal: tell them what to do

options.why: To a friend the imperative is fahr.
Pass … auf, with the prefix at the end.
The imperative of sein is sei.

units.title: Possessivartikel
canDo: say whose something is in any case
use mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser correctly
ask whose something is
units.grammarNote: The full paradigm, now that nominative, accusative and dative all exist. Unit 13 taught the nominative alone; this closes it.

scenario.role: a colleague sorting out whose things are whose
scenario.goal: say who owns what

options.why: Tasche is feminine: unsere Tasche.
Stift is masculine: euer Stift.
gehören takes the dative: meiner Nachbarin.

units.title: Wechselpräpositionen
canDo: choose accusative or dative after in, auf, an
say where something is and where it goes
ask wo or wohin
units.grammarNote: The hardest thing in A1 and correctly last: it needs both cases and the wo/wohin distinction. Movement takes the accusative, position the dative.

scenario.goal: say where things go and where they are

options.why: Movement takes the accusative: auf den Tisch.
No movement, so the dative: an der Wand.
You are moving it there: auf den Tisch.

units.title: Über mich
canDo: introduce yourself for a minute without stopping
say what you did and what you are going to do
ask somebody the same questions back
units.grammarNote: Nothing new. If the forty units worked, this is the unit where you notice.

scenario.goal: introduce yourself properly

options.say: Ich studiere. Mein Beruf kommt später.

options.why: Say it as a sentence: ich studiere.
The verb comes second: am liebsten koche ich.

options.say: Ja, das ist mein Hobby. Und du?
Ja, das ist mein Erfahrung wichtig.
options.why: Erfahrung is feminine, and this says nothing. Keep it simple.
